blocks.content: Missed deadlines covered honestly explaining a specific kind of miss. Wrong decisions widens that to a broader and, in some ways, more nuanced scenario, owning a technical or product decision that turned out wrong, even when the decision itself was reasonably made at the time.

This is a genuinely important distinction from the other failure topics in this module, since a wrong decision is not always the result of carelessness. Sometimes it is a reasonable call that simply did not hold up as new information emerged later, and how you talk about that distinction matters a great deal.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022950751-961305657.png
blocks.alt: Wrong decisions covers owning a technical or product call that turned out wrong, even when it was reasonably made at the time

blocks.content: 1. A Bad Decision Versus a Good Decision That Turned Out Wrong
blocks.text: 1. A Bad Decision Versus a Good Decision That Turned Out Wrong

blocks.content: This distinction is worth making explicit before anything else. A bad decision was made carelessly, with poor process, ignoring information that was genuinely available at the time. A good decision that turned out wrong was reasonable given the information available at the time, but new information later revealed it was not actually the best path.

Interviewers are usually not looking for a story where you admit to genuine carelessness, they are looking for the second kind, a reasonable decision that did not hold up, and how maturely you handled that outcome.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022952676-257633173.png
blocks.alt: A bad decision was made carelessly; a good decision that turned out wrong was reasonable at the time, but new information later changed the picture

blocks.content: 2. Why This Question Gets Asked Specifically
blocks.text: 2. Why This Question Gets Asked Specifically

blocks.content: A few real things get evaluated here. Whether you can admit a call was wrong without excessive defensiveness, since defending an outcome long after it clearly was not the right call is a real red flag. Whether you actually revisit and update decisions as new information arrives, rather than sticking to a path purely out of consistency or ego.

And this question reveals your actual decision making process, not just the final outcome, since a well reasoned decision that turned out wrong is a very different signal than a careless one that happened to work out.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022954361-278542154.png
blocks.alt: This question tests whether you can admit a wrong call without defensiveness, whether you update decisions with new information, and your real process

3. A Worked Example

A concrete story shows this distinction clearly. A simpler technical approach was chosen over a more scalable one specifically to move faster, a reasonable tradeoff given the information available at the time.

First person quote: "I chose a simpler technical approach over a more scalable one, specifically to move faster and ship sooner, which felt like the right tradeoff given our timeline and the usage numbers we had at the time. Usage ended up growing faster than our original estimate anticipated, and the simpler approach became a real bottleneck sooner than expected. I recognized this early, through monitoring, not after it became an actual crisis, and proposed and led a planned migration to the more scalable approach before it turned into a real incident."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022956897-371579450.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: a reasonable tradeoff at the time, recognizing early through monitoring that it no longer held, and leading a planned migration before a crisis

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Only telling the part of the story where the decision was made, without describing how you recognized it needed to change and what you did about it. The recognition and correction are usually the more important half of the story.
4. Judging With Hindsight Versus Foresight

A subtle but important part of telling this story well is being fair to your own past reasoning. Judging the original decision using only information available in hindsight, information that simply was not available at the time, produces an unfair, distorted self assessment, since it makes a reasonable decision look careless in retrospect.

Judging the decision using only the information genuinely available at the time produces a fair, honest self assessment, this was the reasonable choice given what we knew then, and here is what changed. This framing is usually more accurate, and also more credible to an interviewer who can tell the difference.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022958441-87976224.png
blocks.alt: Judging a decision purely through hindsight produces an unfair self assessment; judging it through the information available at the time is fair and honest

blocks.content: 5. What Matters Once New Information Arrives
blocks.text: 5. What Matters Once New Information Arrives

blocks.content: The real test in this topic often comes after the original decision, once new information arrives. Recognizing that the new information genuinely changes the calculus, rather than dismissing it to avoid revisiting a settled decision. Being willing to reverse or adjust course, even publicly, which can feel uncomfortable but is usually the right call.

And not defending the original decision purely out of ego, since the goal was always the best outcome, not being right about the original call forever. This willingness to update is often the actual signal an interviewer is listening for in this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022959995-438975004.png
blocks.alt: What matters once new information arrives: recognizing it changes the calculus, being willing to adjust course, and not defending the original call out of ego

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The willingness to publicly reverse a decision once new information justifies it is usually seen as a sign of strength, not weakness, by a thoughtful interviewer.
6. Genuinely Common Failure Modes

A few real patterns undermine this kind of story. Insisting the original decision was actually right despite a clear outcome suggesting otherwise, which reads as defensive rather than reflective. Blaming the information available at the time on someone else, rather than owning the decision as your own call.
Delaying the course correction well past when the new information was actually clear, which turns a reasonable original decision into a genuinely avoidable, prolonged problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784022961629-921060270.png
blocks.alt: Common failure modes: insisting the decision was right despite the outcome, blaming the information on others, and delaying course correction too long

blocks.content: 7. Choosing Your Own Wrong Decision Story
blocks.text: 7. Choosing Your Own Wrong Decision Story

blocks.content: Look for a decision that was genuinely reasonable given the information available at the time, not a careless one, but where the outcome later showed it was not the best path, and where you can clearly describe how you recognized that and adjusted course.

The strongest stories here show both halves clearly, the reasonable original reasoning and the honest recognition and correction afterward, since a story with only one half feels incomplete to a listening interviewer.
A decision can be reasonable and still turn out wrong. What matters is what you do once you know that.
